Customer: provide sample P95 workload trace and input histogram by 2025-04-14
SE/Ravi: run KV-cache + batching config test with 1.5x traffic by 2025-04-16

summary: Weekly POC sync to review latency and throughput benchmarks vs baseline provider. Redwood shows ~25-35% lower median latency at comparable cost for the 512-token profile when using KV-cache + batching; tail latencies still a concern under bursty traffic. Discussed tuning (batching thresholds, quantization tradeoffs), Dedicated capacity options, and next steps to run customer-specific traffic replay and to share detailed logs and pricing.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-09 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood CSM); Ethan (BlueWave Head of ML), Priya (Platform Eng), Jordan (SRE)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll go about 45 minutes, quick agenda is benchmark review, dig into latency/throughput, and agree next steps. is the timing still good for you folks?
[00:12] Ethan: yup this works, thanks Maya. excited to see the numbers.
[00:20] Ravi: cool, i'll screen share the benchmark dashboard — apologies if the auto transcription spellings in the notes get weird, we call out the baseline provider as 'AcmeBaseline' for anonymity in the sheet.
[01:05] Ravi: ok so slide one is our baseline comparison, tests were run with 512-token generation, mixed temperature, beam=1; baseline is the customer's current vendor (BaselineProvider) running a 4-shard setup. the important rows are median latency, p95, and throughput at 80% CPU util.
[02:10] Priya: quick question — when you say 512-token, is that total tokens or prompt plus generation? our workload is prompt heavy so prompt length is often 150-250 tokens plus ~200-300 generation.
[02:30] Ravi: great callout — the 512 is end-to-end; we've annotated the sheet with prompt vs gen distribution, i'll flag the more representative 350-gen / 200-prompt slice in the shared CSV.
[03:05] Ravi: median latencies: baseline 220ms per token, Redwood hosted profile 160ms per token, Redwood with KV-cache warmed shows 130ms per token on median. p95 is trickier: baseline p95 480ms, Redwood hosted 390ms, with dedicated-like config and warmed cache 320ms. throughput (tokens/s) at sustained load: baseline 6.8k toks/s, Redwood 8.9k toks/s, warmed 10.5k toks/s.
[04:12] Jordan: those numbers look promising but in our spikes we saw p99 outages last week — did you run burst tests?
[04:30] Ravi: yes we did a 3x traffic burst test for 5 minutes. Redwood's smart routing dropped to a lower-cost model variant in one region which added ~200ms; we have a planned follow-up to pin routing during bursts for the pilot.
[05:05] Ethan: cost parity question — is Redwood's lower latency at same cost or requires higher config?
[05:20] Maya: good one. the baseline cost line in the spreadsheet is the effective per-token cost the customer reported. Redwood's hosted numbers map to roughly the same cost at the tier we tested; when you warm cache and use batching the unit cost goes down so you actually get lower cost with better latency in many of the profiles. we'll include a per-model, per-config cost breakdown.
[06:00] Priya: any differences in quantization? our baseline is using 4-bit q8 type quantization and we heard Redwood recommends a different quant profile for some models.
[06:20] Ravi: right, we tested two q profiles — qb4 and qb8 (sorry approximations) — qb4 runs slightly faster but we observed a small delta in generation quality on niche prompts. we didn't see wholesale regression but we'll surface the eval doc.
[07:05] Maya: can you unpause the transcript for the actual csv and the benchmarks?
[07:12] Ravi: sure sharing now — link dropped in chat: https://redwood-internal/share/benchmarks/bwa-2025-04-09.csv (note: link is placeholder).
[07:40] Ethan: looking at the per-sequence breakdown, the 128-256 prompt length group has the biggest delta in throughput. any idea why?
[07:55] Ravi: that's due to batching efficiency — shorter sequences allow higher effective batching ratios which improves GPU utilization. we can tune batching thresholds to favor the longer sequences you guys have.
[09:02] Priya: what about KV cache warmup? our request pattern in production often has lots of cold starts for new users.
[09:20] Ravi: kv-cache warmup matters a lot. our tests show warming the prefix cache reduces token latencies by ~25% median. we also have an optional prefetch strategy to proactively populate KV for target cohorts; it's something we can enable for the pilot and observe impact.
[10:05] Jordan: curious about tail — p99 improved by 15% but we still see some 1s spikes during background GC or when autoscaler spins up nodes. is that expected?
[10:25] Ravi: yes some of that is autoscaler churn. on Dedicated you get reserved capacity which eliminates most autoscaler-induced tails; on hosted we can set burst capacity and keep a warm pool, there are tradeoffs (cost vs guaranteed tail).
[11:00] Maya: maybe we should map this to your SLA needs — Ethan, you had mentioned 99th under 600ms as a target?
[11:15] Ethan: correct, p99 under 600ms and sustained throughput of ~9k toks/s for our peak.
[11:25] Ravi: with the warmed-cache config we're hitting ~10.5k toks/s sustained and p99 around 420-520ms in our sim; so we can meet the target but we'd recommend a small dedicated pool to reduce risk for spikes.
[12:02] Priya: how disruptive is migrating to Dedicated? downtime? config change?
[12:20] Maya: minimal, Dedicated is effectively reserved capacity you can route traffic to; onboarding is a config flip and can be staged with canary. we'll schedule a maintenance window if you require.
[12:45] Ethan: what about security/compliance — we need SOC2 type II and SSO with SAML; is that covered for the pilot?
[12:55] Sofia: yes, Redwood has SOC2 and SAML SSO for enterprise; for pilot we can provide masked logs and scoped retention. i'll share the security pack after the call.
[13:30] Ravi: back to perf, one more nuance — we saw that ModelVariant A (faster kernels) has better median but slightly worse on certain long-context prompts due to attention kernel differences. we included model-variant mapping in the sheet.
[14:05] Ethan: can you re-run the benchmark with our real traffic trace? we want to see exact tail behavior.
[14:20] Ravi: absolutely, please drop the trace in the shared folder. we can replay at 1x and 1.5x and give you logs with request ids.
[15:00] Priya: on the replay, will the KV cache be representative? we don't want optimistic warm caches that don't reflect cold-starts.
[15:15] Ravi: good point — we'll provide both cold and warm replay runs and label them. the 'cold' run wipes prefix caches between sessions.
[16:00] Jordan: any concerns about model semantic drift with quantization? some of our legal prompts are pretty sensitive to hallucinations.
[16:20] Ravi: we can run evals on your safety prompt set and include per-variant quality scores. if a quant profile introduces regression we'll note it; you can always pin to higher precision for legal flows.
[17:03] Ethan: you mentioned smart routing earlier, can we pin to specific regions? latency to EU users is important.
[17:20] Maya: yes you can pin routing by region and by model variant. we also support regional Dedicated pools.
[18:05] Priya: show us the cost breakdown per 1M tokens again?
[18:20] Ravi: baseline reported $X per 1M tokens (anonymized), Redwood hosted at tested tier is roughly the same; when using batching+cache the effective cost drops ~18%. we'll attach a csv with the per-config cost math.
[19:00] Ethan: what configuration gave you the 10.5k toks/s number?
[19:12] Ravi: that was hosted with warmed KV, batch size target 128, latency SLO 200ms and seq-sharding enabled on the runtime.
[20:05] Priya: will seq-sharding affect concurrency for individual requests?
[20:20] Ravi: it affects how the runtime partitions long sequences across GPUs for throughput; for short sequences it increases throughput without harming single-request latency. there's tuning knobs.
[21:00] Maya: ok let's talk risks: client side — workload variance, sudden spikes; provider side — autoscaler churn, variant fallback. mitigations are: dedicated pool, pinned routing, warm pool, and run replay tests.
[22:05] Ethan: agreed. for pilot success we want: p99 < 600ms, sustained 9k toks/s on your replay, and no quality regression on our legal prompt set.
[22:30] Maya: sounds good. we'll run the replay at 1x and 1.5x and send results by 2025-04-16.
[23:00] Ravi: i'll also include raw logs and an annotated step-by-step of the perf config used (batch thresholds, seq-shard, cache warm policy).
[23:35] Priya: any configuration that requires code changes on our side?
[23:50] Ravi: no code changes, mainly runtime flags and routing config. the only optional integration is a small prefetch hook if you want to proactively populate caches from your side — that's a script we can provide.
[24:30] Ethan: one last quick thing — during the 3x burst test, you mentioned a fallback to a cheaper model variant, can that fallback be disabled for the pilot?
[24:45] Ravi: yes, we can disable automatic variant fallback for forward-facing traffic and fall back to regional capacity policies instead. that increases cost exposure on bursts but keeps latency predictable.
[25:30] Maya: ok recap of next steps: Maya to send pricing + tier options, Ravi to run replay and upload logs, Ethan to share traces and prompt set. we should meet again next week same time to review replay results.
[25:55] Jordan: works for us.
[26:10] Sofia: i'll also share the security pack and scoping doc right after this call.
[26:30] Ethan: thanks everyone — overall these numbers look encouraging.
[26:45] Maya: thanks team, we'll follow up in email with links, talk to you next week.
[27:00] (call ends)

Notes: the transcription above includes some mis-hearings and shorthand; refer to the shared benchmark CSV for exact numeric rows.
